title: Networks: VPC, subnets and endpoints
bridge: A VPC is like your office network: your own address range, rooms called subnets, and a router table. Except 'private' in AWS means there is no route out, not that a firewall blocks the traffic. The firewall is a separate thing, the security group on each machine.
intro: A sandbox VM reads untrusted text, so it must have no way to send our code anywhere. This lesson builds the network for that: private subnets, no internet gateway, no NAT. Then it opens only the doors a VM needs. Those are endpoints to AWS services, the proxy, and DNS for a short list of names.

picture.caption: Inside the sandbox VPC every packet follows the route table; only named doors lead anywhere.

steps.text: sends a packet; the route table decides where it may go
S3 traffic goes to the gateway endpoint; its policy allows only our buckets
AWS API calls (SSM, ECR, logs) go to private IPs inside the VPC, port 443
every name lookup passes the DNS firewall; names off the list get NXDOMAIN
web traffic for allowed names goes to the proxy on port 3128
only the proxy has a route to the internet (p4-5)
no 0.0.0.0/0 route: any other packet to the internet has nowhere to go

sections.h: Start from the network you are on
p: Your laptop has a private address, like 192.168.1.23, given by your home router. The router knows one extra route: anything that is not local goes to the internet. Remove that route and your laptop still talks to the printer, but nothing else.
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is that home network inside AWS. You choose its address range and you write every route yourself. Nothing leaves unless a route says where.
sections.because: We look at your own routes first because a VPC route table works the same way.

code.text:
ipconfig getifaddr en0          # your private address on Wi-Fi
netstat -rn -f inet | head -4   # your route table
# 'default' is the route to the internet, through your router

notes.text: en0 is usually the Wi-Fi card on a Mac. The address is private: it only means something at home.
The route table: for each destination, where to send the packet.
The line starting with default is the way out. A sandbox subnet has no such line.

sections.h: CIDR: an address range in one line
p: A CIDR block writes a range as a start address and a size. 10.60.0.0/16 means the first 16 bits are fixed: every address from 10.60.0.0 to 10.60.255.255, 65,536 in all. A bigger number after the slash means a smaller range: a /18 holds 16,384, a /28 holds 16.

G3-04 gives the sandbox VPC 10.60.0.0/16, a range no other network of ours uses. G3-03 cuts it into four /18s: three for VMs, one per AZ, and the fourth kept for the proxy. OpenTofu's cidrsubnet() does the cutting, and you can try it without any cloud.
sections.because: We compute subnets with cidrsubnet() because hand-typed ranges overlap sooner or later.

code.text:
echo 'cidrsubnet("10.60.0.0/16", 2, 0)' | tofu console
echo '[for n in range(3) : cidrsubnet("10.60.0.0/16", 2, n)]' | tofu console
echo 'cidrsubnet(cidrsubnet("10.60.0.0/16", 2, 3), 10, 0)' | tofu console

notes.text: Add 2 bits to /16 to get a /18, and take block number 0 of the four.
The three VM subnets, exactly the expression in modules/aws-vpc-private.
Take the fourth /18, add 10 more bits (a /28), take the first: a proxy subnet (G3-09).

p: A subnet is a slice of the VPC's range in one AZ. Each subnet uses a route table. A new VPC's route table has one route: the VPC's own range goes to 'local'.

A public subnet adds 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway (IGW), the VPC's door to the internet. A private subnet in most VPCs adds 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway, which lets machines call out but not be called. Our modules/aws-vpc builds both, with public IPs on launch.
Sandboxes get neither. G3-03 copies the module as aws-vpc-private: no public subnets, no IGW, no NAT, no public IPs. The SCP from p3-1 stops anyone adding a NAT later.
sections.because: We build the VPC by hand once so the route table you read later in Terraform is not a mystery.

code.text:
VPC=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.60.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text)
for i in 0 1 2; do
  aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.60.$((i * 64)).0/18 \
    --availability-zone us-east-1$(echo abc | cut -c$((i + 1))) \
    --query 'Subnet.[SubnetId,CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone]' --output text
done
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC \
  --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[]' --output table

notes.text: Creates the VPC and keeps its ID in a shell variable.
One per AZ: us-east-1a, b and c.
Reads the routes. There is only the local one: no way out.

sections.h: Gateway endpoint: S3 without the internet
p: A VPC endpoint is a private door from your VPC to an AWS service. The S3 kind is a gateway endpoint. It adds a route to a prefix list, AWS's named list of S3's address ranges. S3 traffic then stays inside AWS.

An endpoint has its own policy. The current modules/aws-vpc allows '*', so a VM could use a presigned URL to anyone's bucket. That is a way out for our code. G3-03 allows only our buckets: the runs bucket, and the bucket where ECR keeps image layers.
sections.because: We list buckets in the endpoint policy because an open S3 endpoint is an exit to every bucket in the world.

notes.text: Anyone inside the VPC, because the VM has no AWS identity of its own for S3 (p3-6).
Read and write objects. No list, no delete, no bucket settings.
Our runs bucket, where presigned uploads go (p3-6).
ECR stores image layers in this AWS-owned bucket. Without it, docker pull from ECR fails.

sections.h: Interface endpoints: private doors to AWS APIs
p: Most AWS services use interface endpoints instead. Each one is a network card with a private IP in your subnets. With private DNS on, a name like ssm.us-east-1.amazonaws.com resolves to that private IP inside the VPC.

G3-04 lists what a sandbox needs. ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages let the SSM agent take commands (p3-5). ecr.api and ecr.dkr let Docker pull our images. logs sends logs, and autoscaling lets a VM finish its lifecycle hook (p3-4). A security group lets in port 443 from the VPC only.
sections.because: We create one interface endpoint by hand because the other six differ only in the service name.

code.text:
ESG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name endpoints \
  --description "443 from the VPC" --vpc-id $VPC --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $ESG --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 10.60.0.0/16
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id $VPC --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ssm --private-dns-enabled \
  --subnet-ids $(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'Subnets[].SubnetId' --output text) \
  --security-group-ids $ESG --query 'VpcEndpoint.[VpcEndpointType,ServiceName]' --output text

notes.text: A security group for the endpoints themselves.
Only HTTPS, only from addresses inside the VPC.
The service name is com.amazonaws.<region>.<service>. Private DNS makes the normal name point here.
One network card per subnet, so each AZ has its own copy.

sections.ifInstead: If instead you see InvalidSubnetID.NotFound with three IDs in one string, your shell did not split them. Keep the $( ) inline as shown; zsh does not split a variable.

sections.h: Security groups: a firewall on each VM
p: A security group is a firewall attached to a machine's network card. Ingress rules say what may come in; egress rules say what may go out. It is stateful: replies to an allowed request always get back.

G3-11's sandbox group has no ingress at all: nobody can connect to a sandbox. Egress goes only to the proxy on 3128, the endpoints on 443, and the PrivateLink endpoint to our services on inf (p4-5). A new group allows all egress by default, so step one is to remove that rule.
sections.because: We revoke the default egress rule first because a new security group lets everything out.

code.text:
SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name sandbox \
  --description "sandbox: no ingress" --vpc-id $VPC --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-egress --group-id $SG \
  --ip-permissions '[{"IpProtocol":"-1","IpRanges":[{"CidrIp":"0.0.0.0/0"}]}]'
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-egress --group-id $SG \
  --ip-permissions '[{"IpProtocol":"tcp","FromPort":3128,"ToPort":3128,"IpRanges":[{"CidrIp":"10.60.192.0/24"}]}]'
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids $SG \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[0].[length(IpPermissions), IpPermissionsEgress[0].FromPort]' --output text

notes.text: A new group has no ingress rules. We never add one.
Removes the default 'all traffic to anywhere' egress rule.
Allows TCP 3128 to the proxy's range only. In G3-11 the target is the proxy's network load balancer (NLB), not a whole /24.
0 ingress rules, and the one egress port is 3128.

callout.text: Security groups have no deny rules. To block something, you remove the allow. That is why the default egress rule must go.

sections.h: DNS firewall: the last quiet way out
p: Even with no route out, a VM can ask the VPC's DNS resolver for a name. The resolver asks the internet on the VM's behalf. A lookup for c2VjcmV0.attacker.com carries data in the name itself: that is DNS exfiltration.

G3-04 closes it with Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall. One domain list holds the allowed names: the proxy allow-list, *.amazonaws.com and *.ai-agents.example.com. An ALLOW rule lets those through; a BLOCK rule answers NXDOMAIN ('no such name') for everything else. Queries are logged to CloudWatch.
G3-04 also adds a private DNS zone, ai-agents.example.com, visible only inside the VPC. It holds proxy., broker., gateway. and otel. names.
sections.because: We block DNS by default because a lookup is the one packet that leaves even when no route does.

code.file: AWS CLI shape from the Route 53 Resolver docs (moto does not emulate this part)
code.text:
LIST=$(aws route53resolver create-firewall-domain-list --name allowed \
  --creator-request-id allowed-1 --query FirewallDomainList.Id --output text)
aws route53resolver update-firewall-domains --firewall-domain-list-id $LIST --operation ADD \
  --domains nexus.example.com '*.amazonaws.com' '*.ai-agents.example.com'
ALL=$(aws route53resolver create-firewall-domain-list --name everything \
  --creator-request-id everything-1 --query FirewallDomainList.Id --output text)
aws route53resolver update-firewall-domains --firewall-domain-list-id $ALL --operation ADD --domains '*'
GROUP=$(aws route53resolver create-firewall-rule-group --name sandbox-dns \
  --creator-request-id group-1 --query FirewallRuleGroup.Id --output text)
aws route53resolver create-firewall-rule --firewall-rule-group-id $GROUP --firewall-domain-list-id $LIST \
  --priority 100 --action ALLOW --name allow-list --creator-request-id rule-1
aws route53resolver create-firewall-rule --firewall-rule-group-id $GROUP --firewall-domain-list-id $ALL \
  --priority 200 --action BLOCK --block-response NXDOMAIN --name block-rest --creator-request-id rule-2
aws route53resolver associate-firewall-rule-group --firewall-rule-group-id $GROUP --vpc-id $VPC \
  --priority 101 --name sandbox-vpc --creator-request-id assoc-1

notes.text: A domain list is a named set of names. creator-request-id makes a retried call safe.
The allowed names. Today the proxy list is only nexus.example.com (p4-5).
A second list with '*', meaning every name.
Lower priority numbers run first: allowed names match here and stop.
Everything else gets NXDOMAIN, as if the name did not exist.
Attaches the rules to the sandbox VPC. G3-04 does all of this in Terraform.

quiz.q: A subnet's route table has no 0.0.0.0/0 route. What does that mean for its VMs?

options.text: A firewall drops their internet traffic and logs it
options.why: No firewall is involved. Packets have no route; flow logs and security groups are separate.

options.text: Packets to the internet have nowhere to go; local traffic and endpoints still work
options.why: Private in AWS means no route out. The local route and endpoint routes still apply.

options.text: The VMs cannot start until a NAT gateway exists
options.why: VMs start fine in private subnets; they only lack a path out.

quiz.q: Why does the S3 gateway endpoint policy list our buckets and nothing else?

options.text: S3 charges extra for endpoint traffic to other buckets
options.why: Gateway endpoints cost nothing; the reason is security.

options.text: Without the list, our own bucket would not be reachable
options.why: An open policy reaches our bucket too. The list closes the others.

options.text: Otherwise a presigned URL to anyone's bucket would work from inside: a way out for our code
options.why: That is the gap G3-03 names in the current module, which allows '*'.

quiz.q: No IGW and no NAT. How could data still leave the VPC, and what closes that?

options.text: In DNS lookups that carry data in the name; the DNS firewall answers NXDOMAIN for names off the list
options.why: The resolver asks the internet for the VM. The firewall stops that for any name not allowed.

options.text: Through ICMP pings; the security group closes that
options.why: Pings to the internet have no route either.

options.text: Through the interface endpoints; the SCP closes that
options.why: Interface endpoints reach AWS services in our account and region, not arbitrary hosts.

words.plain: A private network in AWS with your own address range, subnets and route tables.
An address range written as start/size, like 10.60.0.0/16; a bigger number after the slash is a smaller range.
A slice of the VPC's range in one availability zone.
The list that tells a subnet where packets for each destination go; no 0.0.0.0/0 route means no way out.
A private door to an AWS service: a route (gateway kind, S3) or a private IP (interface kind).
A stateful firewall on a machine's network card, with allow rules only.
Route 53 Resolver rules that answer only allowed names and NXDOMAIN for the rest.

tickets.why: The private-only VPC module: three /18s, no IGW or NAT, an S3 endpoint limited to our buckets, interface endpoints.
Builds the sandbox network in the ai-agents account: 10.60.0.0/16, DNS firewall, private zone and the runs bucket.
The sandbox security group: no ingress, egress only to the proxy, the endpoints and PrivateLink.

remember: Private means no route out. Then open only named doors: endpoints for AWS, and the proxy and DNS for one short list.
